And then I called the general manager at the headquarters in Bjelovar. Then I left Pakrac and went to meet Professor Jovan Raskovic, who was the president of SDS. I complained to him about the ultimatum, and he immediately asked me to go and find refuge in Serbia, because people had already arrived from Knin to inquire about me. So that I should go away in order to save my head for a while until he made some arrangements. I went to Vrnjacka Banja, and after eight or nine days, the professor called me to come back, and then we talked and he told me that I could return and that he believed that there was no danger any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after you returned to Pakrac, what happened on the 12th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: On my return to Pakrac, due to the events which were going on both in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja where war was raging, we made the decision to form the SAO Western Slavonia with only one purpose, that the area would distance itself from the events in Eastern Slavonia and in Baranja. And when we formed the SAO Western Slavonia, we would try to negotiate with Croatian authorities and thereby try to avoid possible conflict and the war which was already at our door.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we talked about the establishment of the SAO for the SBWS. Had you in Western Slavonia been consulted or participated in the Eastern Slavonia initiative?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The initiative of the Eastern Slavonia is something we did not participate in. When I heard that it was formed, I asked Goran Hadzic why we hadn't been included in these arrangements, and then he told me that they did not have enough time for that but that they had space and room for us to be involved in their institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you wish to be involved in their institutions?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: No, we did not want to participate in their institutions. Because the moment when Goran Hadzic told me that he was going to war and that the war option was the only solution for him, I talked with my political associates, and we made the decision that we would establish our own SAO Western Slavonia so that it wouldn't be under the wing of anyone else's policy and so that nobody else would think that we were part of the war option. We were doing anything that we could to avoid the war and try to reach a peaceful resolution through dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we call up 65 ter 2819. It's a map. Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, if you could, just indicate with the pen for us the territory of the SAO Western Slavonia as it was envisioned or declared.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This in blue was the envisaged Western Slavonia where in our view Serbs made up the ethnic majority, a relative one or perhaps even an absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And new we're getting ahead just a little bit. But to the end of 1991, at the end of 1991, can you indicate what's the territory of Western Slavonia that was actually controlled or held by the Serb people there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In late 1991, we can see here -- I will indicate it with a red line. This was the area of the Western Slavonia that was under the control of the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that was actually the territory that was held.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So, for the record, the larger area being the declared territory, and the smaller area that's been marked is the area that was actually held by the Serb people there at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we'll have a problem with this marking because there are red marks all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me -- I understand. Perhaps I could do it a different way that would make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can the registrar take those markings off and we'll start over again. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, can you indicate with a number 1 the area that was the territory of the SAO Western Slavonia as declared or as envisioned? Put a number 1 in the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then perhaps using a line, you could make a number 2 and then point with the line to the area that you've just described which was the territory actually held inside the red border.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honour, we tender this map. If it could be given a new number now and tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2819 marked by the witness in court shall be assigned Exhibit Number P23. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzakula, you indicated that the government of SAO Western Slavonia was formed to negotiate with the Croatian government. Was there a primary contact person or interlocutor that you had dealings with who was in the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The contacts were focused on Mr. Degoricija and Mr. Lerotic who was an advisor to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the position of Mr. Degoricija?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: He was the assistant minister of the interior, but President Tudjman had assigned him to hold talks with Serbs in all areas in order to try and find a resolution without a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after the SAO Western Slavonia was formed on the 12th of August, 1991, could you describe for the Chamber how the government was formed and the extent to which it was able to function in the area of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The government of the SAO Western Slavonia was founded on the 12th of August. As for the members, there were several members of the Regional Boards of SDS from Daruvar, Okucani, Pakrac, Podravska Slatina with the goal that the political body should try to find a political resolution through dialogue. The government itself never met after it was formed, nor did it ever pass or adopt any documents or regulations or laws. It was a political body which attempted to find a resolution. The actual power in the area was the Territorial Defence with its staffs and commands in all municipalities and at the regional level. They had the actual power because, due to the conflicts and after the conflicts which broke out, they formed the civilian authorities. And as time went by and as their influence diminished because they were losing territories, their power diminished, and our authority was growing, because everyone was looking for a way out of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In a few sentences, if you could just describe for Your Honours the incident that occurred on the 14th of August, 1991, two days after the SAO Western Slavonia was declared.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: After the declaration of the SAO Western Slavonia, we were convinced that we would find a peaceful resolution. However, in the morning of the 14th of August in Okucani and also in Grubisno Polje, so it means in the north and in the south of Western Slavonia, incidents between the Croatian police and the citizens of Serbian ethnicity began. Those incidents in the area of Okucani grew into a widespread conflict in which the JNA which arrived from Daruvar and Bjelovar was also involved, and this lasted up until -- for two or three days. So these two incidents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. Witness, could you slow down a little bit. You're going too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All right. Thank you. I will. Such incidents, which began with conflict, disturbed the Serbian population additionally. And on the 19th of August, a widespread conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, on the day -- you mentioned the conflict breaking out there on the 19th of August. Did something happen the day before, on the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: On the previous day, I was arrested and taken to Kraguj village to Jovo Vezmar. He was putting on a JNA uniform and he informed me that they were going to war, and I should make up my mind whether I was with them or against them. Because if I were against them, I would be killed, and I should be very careful about what I would do on the following days. So I was kept there in a house, in a sort of home detention, and in the morning on the 19th of August, I was taken in front of the staff of Territorial Defence in Branesci village where I saw a big confusion. There many people in uniforms who were preparing themselves to start an attack against Pakrac. Some people shouted that I was a traitor, that they should kill me and what was I doing there, and the man who was standing there did not forbid them to shout, but he didn't allow them to fight with me. Around 5.00 a.m., they took me from there to Dereza village, and people were living it to go into combat. They were frightened. They didn't know what was going on. They asked me what was going on, and I told them, "Well, you see that the war is going on. Be careful. Don't kill anyone without any reason whatsoever. Be very careful and wary." And the man who was next to me said, "Shut up. You have no right to speak." And he took me back to Branesci, and the war really began.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to a man named Vezmar. Is it the same person you'd been taken to before in July?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same person they took me to on the 15th of July. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff in Pakrac on the 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after the conflict began, did you have any interaction or participate in the conflict yourself or with the TO that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I did not take part in the conflict. I was a silent observer, watching from the sides as far as I was allowed to. I tried to make contacts with the Territorial Defence during the lulls. I met with a few people from the Pozega municipality in Dragovic. We talked because they recognised me. They asked me what was going on, and I told them, "Well, you see the war was broken out, so make sure that in the war you do not commit any crimes because you will be held responsible sooner or later." After I said that, on the following day, I was summoned again to the Command of the Western Slavonia staff where I was met by Veljko Vukelic and Jovo Vezmar. And, once again, Jovo Vezmar told me, "I'm telling you once again not to spread defeatism among our soldiers because if you continue to do that we will liquidate you." And after that, I did not have any contacts of the kind with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 65 ter Exhibit 408. This is tab 13. This is a short document, so I think we can work with it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I don't know yet if you've mentioned the Serbian Radical Party. Can you tell us what the Serbian Radical Party was.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, we did mention the Serbian Radical Party and its president Vojislav Seselj. The Serbian Radical Party, inter alia, tried to enlist volunteers in Serbia and send them to the front in Eastern Slavonia and Western Slavonia and also to the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just in the upper left-hand corner, where is Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Podravska Slatina is in the north-western Slavonia close to the Hungarian border to the north of the Pozega municipality and the neighbouring Virovitica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this document is -- the subject is a request for help and manpower directed to the Serbian Radical Party in Belgrade. The question here is whether at any time you became aware or heard that Serbian Radical Party volunteers had come to fight in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that they did come, because Ilija Sasic, who was from Western Slavonia, from Podravska Slatina, was in close contact with Vojislav Seselj, and he made sure that their volunteers would come to that particular area in order to help their Territorial Defence in the combat and the war which were ongoing in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We can just set that aside. I've got a few more of these that I'd like to show the witness, Your Honour, and then I can tender the group of them. The next is 65 ter 425.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you see that well enough on the screen, Mr. Dzakula? It's a bit faded, the original language version.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to look at this document before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber just in a couple of sentences what -- what this is.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: It's a document from the staff of Western Slavonia reporting about the Western Slavonia area, and the seven municipal staffs which are listed by municipality - Grubisno Polje, Pakrac, Daruvar, Pozega, Okucani, Novska and others - with the names of commanders and commanders of smaller units who were involved in staffs according to their functions. The names of units, battalions, companies. This is a detailed overview and a description of the military forces through the staffs of municipalities and towns who were members of the staff of Western Slavonia and who were involved in direct combat with the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the very top of the second page of this document in your version, and in English it's just about a quarter of the way down. That's a reference to the Municipal Staff TO Pakrac. And you see the name, Commander Vezmar, Jovo.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Jovo Vezmar was the commander of the TO staff in Pakrac. It was the same man who was the chief of the police in Pakrac up until the 2nd of March and who, on the 15th of July, gave me the ultimatum to leave Pakrac and who, on the 18th of August, arrested me in order to let me know that they were going to war. So this is the very same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if at any time Mr. Vezmar held a position in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovo Vezmar escaped to Serbia after the 2nd of March, to Pancevo, where he worked in the police. He was some sort of chief or inspector. He came to the front in Western Slavonia. And at some point in late October, he left Western Slavonia, and once again he returned to the Serbian MUP in Pancevo. Later on he was retired from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when you said 2nd of March and then late October, what year or years are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: All of that happened in 1991. What happened on the 2nd of March and also in October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter 462.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzakula, the first document in this series we looked at was dated the 16th of October, 1991. That was number 425. Excuse me. It was 408, dated the 12th of October, 1991. This one, again, has the reference to the Podravska Slatina TO. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, again, going to the Serbian Radical Party in Belgrade. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So then is this -- is this further to your testimony or related to your testimony about having learned of Serbian Radical Party volunteers coming to fight in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it's connected with the same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the next document is 65 ter 714. Mr. Dzakula, where is Novska?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Novska is to the south-west of Slavonia, at the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina. So both -- there's Okucani, and then to the right from Okucani towards Zagreb is Novska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is another request coming from the TO staff, a TO staff, for volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party. There's a reference here to -- directly to Dr. Seselj. My question is whether you know or heard if Dr. Seselj himself personally came into the Western Slavonia region during the conflict there in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a document which was also sent to the Radical Party, Mr. Vojvoda Dr. Seselj requesting assistance. Vojislav Seselj did visit Western Slavonia in late October, at some point in October 1991, and he went precisely to the Vocin and Podravska Slatina area. Zvecevo, Vocin, Podravska Slatina in order to visit his units. He made a tour of inspection, he talked to them, and he was accompanied by the commander of the staff of the Western Slavonia TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, the documents we've been looking at cover the period October, I think, to -- October and November. You said the conflict began on the 19th of August. Can you describe just in general terms and briefly can you give an overview of how the conflict played out in Western Slavonia during this period of time and its impact on the civilian populations living inside the area?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: After the incidents on the 14th of August, 1991 which happened in Okucani and Grubisno Polje, on the 19th of August in the morning, there was a general attack of the Serbian Territorial Defence on Pakrac, Novska Gradiska, Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Slatina, Virovitica, Orahovica, that is to say, from all sides. There was an all-out attack. And their goal at the time was to establish some sort of border which would be moved from the Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you think you could --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Should I slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you are going very fast, and I am even wondering, are you reading from a text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I'm not reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was just wondering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat. After the incidents on the 14th of August, 1991, in the area of Okucani and Grubisno Polje, on the 19th of August, there was a general attack by the Serbian Territorial Defence on all the towns in the area from Novska, Nova Gradiska, Pakrac, Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Slatina, Pozega, and Virovitica. I must say then that our commanders thought that the war would last five days, so they did not warn the civilian population about what could happen to them. So many of them, sensing that there would be a conflict, left the towns that I mentioned and took shelter in the villages where the Serbs were a majority in order to wait for the outcome of these events. The war did not proceed in the desired manner and at the pace foreseen by the commanders. It stretched to several weeks and then months. At the very beginning of the war, we had a lot of wounded, but there were no doctors and no hospitals, so that many of the wounded died. They succumbed to their wounds because of bleeding because there was nobody to treat them. It was strange that nobody sent any medical supplies, not even by helicopter. This happened only after 60 days, by which time many had already succumbed to their wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me, if I may, just jump in at this point, Mr. Dzakula, and give you some specific questions. We looked earlier at a map where you indicated the territory of Western Slovenia -- Western Slavonia as it was declared and then the smaller area in which you indicated the area actually held by the Serb TO. Is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this period of time and, indeed, in the months that followed, can you just indicate generally, and we'll talk about it in much more detail, what happened to Croats, if you can generalise, what happened to Croats who found themselves in Serb-controlled areas, and what happened to Serb civilians who now found themselves living in Croat-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In the Western Slavonia area, which was caught up in the war, the villages inhabited by Croats were places where some crimes occurred -- rather, some Croats were killed. And then Bacin and some other villages close to Slatina, as well as the Croats in Vinogradi above Pakrac were victims of crimes by Serbian extremists who used the war in order to take their revenge on those they did not respect or like. The same thing happened to Serb civilians in areas controlled by the Croatian authorities. They were also killed, taken away, arrested, beaten, and liquidated. This happened in Zagreb also and in towns such as Sisak, Gospic, Pakracka Poljana, Daruvar, Gospic. They were taken to Kerestinac, a camp near Zagreb. They were taken to the fair near Zagreb, and also there was a prison in Pakracka Poljana where they were liquidated. Civilians were victims, both Serbs and Croats respectively, in areas either under the control of the Croats or under the control of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution moves into evidence 65 ter 425, 408, 462, and 714.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 408 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P24. 65 ter document 425 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P25. 65 ter document 462 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P26. 65 ter document 714 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P27. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, as a result of these events that you've just described, or at least partially as a result, do you know whether in late 1991 the international community got involved and proposed an agreement or a plan to end the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. In late 1991, I think on the 2nd of December, an agreement was signed. The Vance Plan was proposed, which supposed to provide an option to resolve the conflict that broke out in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask the registrar to put up exhibit 3623, 65 ter 3623. It is tab 19. Now, on this one, Your Honours, the English version is the full document, which is the Security Council Resolution, and attached to which is Annex 3, that is primarily what we're interested in here. So on page 15 of this, that's where we want to go. The -- the translation into the witness's language is only Annex 3. The entire document has not been translated, just the part we're going to ask him to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, just moving ahead into 1992. During 1992, as the president of Western Slavonia, were you involved in discussions -- I should say as -- in 1991 as well, were you involved in discussions about the Vance Plan and did you participate in negotiations and talks involving the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In late 1991, at approximately the 15th of December and on, and then in early 1992, I did take part in talks about accepting the Vance Plan as a peaceful solution for the conflicts which broke out in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And later on, did you actually meet with representatives of the international community on this issue?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Later, in April 1992, I was part of a delegation of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in New York to see Mr. Marrack Goulding, the under-secretary of the United Nations, where -- along with the president -- or the Prime Minister Zecevic and Deputy Prime Minister of Yugoslavia Borislav Jovic and the defence minister of Republika Serbian Krajina, Spanovic, we attended talks on the topic of the Vance Plan and its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber just a general overview or description of the main aspects of the Vance Plan, when it came into being? What were the main points of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, the first thing was to achieve a lasting cease-fire and that forces of the United Nations will deploy inside the RSK territory at the time that was affected by war, that, in agreement with the then-local authorities, the plan would be implemented, primarily implying the demilitarisation, the return of refugees until the final political solution to the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just looking at this document here, the English page 16, we see a reference to United Nations Protected Areas. It's farther down the document in your language, Mr. Dzakula. Let me ask you about that in a moment. The reference here is to protected areas, and you can see they relate to Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia, and Krajina. Do you see those references, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do those protected areas correspond, in general, to the areas of what we're calling the SAOs, the Serbian Autonomous Districts, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, except for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Explain what the difference was for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: According to this peace plan, there were no other municipalities mentioned that were affected by war, and that is Pozega, Orahovac, and Slatina. They were left out. We never found out why that was so. And because of that, we frequently made the objection that those three municipalities as well, due to the war there and the refugees, should also be part of the UN peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you made a reference to demilitarisation. What was to be the role of the -- the peacekeepers coming in, what we're calling the UNPROFOR peacekeepers?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The arrival of the peace forces was supposed to mean that they would be the only military force in that area, that there would be no other armies, and they were supposed to provide lasting protection for the population there and enable the return of the refugees. That meant that the Yugoslav People's Army was to leave that area and that the long barrelled and heavy weaponry was supposed to be placed under the control of the United Nations under a double key, as it was referred to, under the control of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your understanding of the role of the police that was envisioned under the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The way I understood the Vance Plan was the way it was written. Meaning that there would be no military forces, that the long and heavy weaponry would be placed under double key in depots, that the police would be the only armed formation with only short-barrelled weapons, meaning that they would only have their side-arms, no machine-guns, automatic rifles or any other type of long-barrelled weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, would be this be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dzakula, we'll take the break now and come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before the break, my colleague Ms. Clanton very helpfully pointed out that I had skipped over part of my outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so, Mr. Dzakula, I'd like to step back in time just to cover one incident that I meant to cover earlier after we spoke about Plitvice in March of 1991. What happened at Borovo Selo in early May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, 1991, a bus of Croatian police entered Borovo Selo, and then they began to fire at houses. Within a few minutes, there was a response by the people who lived in Borovo Selo. This battle lasted for several hours. And then the Yugoslav People's Army came to help, to protect and pull out the Croatian policemen who were deployed around the fields there and in the local houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, from what you know, was it only local Serbs who were involved in that conflict or were there Serbs present who were from other places?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I heard from the media that there were volunteers of the Chetnik duke Vojislav Seselj in Borovo Selo and that they also took part in that fighting in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we can go back to it if we need to, but do you recall if there was a reference -- if Mr. Seselj made a reference to Borovo Selo in the interview that he'd given that was published in his book which we talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall in that article, and as well as on numerous other occasions, Mr. Seselj said that his volunteers also took part in that fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, for the record, Mr. President, that is the document at tab 7. It was 65 ter 142. I don't recall the exhibit number that it's now been given, but that's the reference that we're making.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Dzakula, just moving now forward again to the Vance Plan where we left off before the break. With the usher's assistance, I'd like you to look at 65 ter Exhibit 770.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And before we do that, the Prosecution moves into evidence the current exhibit which is up, 3623.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Stringer, wouldn't that be something for the law library? I perhaps should specify that it's not only -- well, should those documents be agreed upon or not? Of course when a law is concerned, there can be discussion about the interpretation of the law, but as long as it's not discussed that it is a law that was in force at the moment, I think those documents belong in the law library.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We certainly have no objection to that, Your Honour. This is a Security Council Resolution. The attached -- the annex is the text essentially of the Vance Plan as it's been described by the witness, and no objection to it being marked as a law library exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Has the Defence a position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence position is that all documents should be tendered into exhibits, not through legal library, because the concept of legal library is not known in the Rules of this Tribunal or in the Statute, and it is our position that it should be tendered as all -- all other documents, into exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, there is perhaps a misunderstanding here. If documents are not agreed upon, they have to be tendered and admitted, but the only issue here is whether we give it a P number or an L number, and we would prefer legal documents, texts of laws, et cetera, give them an L number. About this one, the Prosecutor is tendering it, and either we admit it -- we admit and mark it as a P number, or we admit and mark it as an L number. That's the only difference. It's not -- it's not that L documents don't have to be tendered if they're not agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As to -- as to the documents, we mentioned 56 documents earlier, and the Defence agreed with authenticity of these documents, but we have -- we might have some other interpretation of some provisions of these documents. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. No problem about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So this document is admitted and marked as an L document, an L exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3623 becomes Exhibit L2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is marked as 65 ter 770, and that is tab 20. And these are minutes of a long meeting, and I suggest it might be faster and more efficient to provide the witness with the original language version of these in the paper. We're going to be moving around the document quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, do you see -- the document that's in front of you that's been marked as 770, have you had a chance to look at that previously?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did have the chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell the Chamber what this is, what the document is.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: These are minutes from a meeting of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia held on the 9th of December, 1991 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as indicated on the first page of both versions, was Goran Hadzic present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'll mention just another -- a couple other names. Milan Martic, you've mentioned who he was at the time. Was he present?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, he was present. He was minister of the interior of the SAO Krajina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Radovan Karadzic, as well, was present.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, he was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we'll talk about this in a minute, but Milan Babic, who you've already described, was not present, nor was Slobodan Milosevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I do. Milan Babic did not attend the meeting, nor did Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall what one of the main reasons or topics for discussion was at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The main topic was the Vance Plan, how to accept it, to discuss it, what it represented, what options for protection it provided, what would be the good solutions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we see Branko Kostic here is vice-president of the SFRY Presidency at the time. Did he essentially chair the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. He was present, and he chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the first ten or so pages, then, of the transcript that follow, and we're for the going to talk about them specifically, but this appears to be an overview that Mr. Kostic gave regarding various aspects of the Vance Plan that was being proposed at the time. What I'd like to do is direct you first to page 18, Mr. Dzakula, of your version, page 13 of the English. And, in this part, Mr. Kostic is still speaking, and he says -- this is about two-thirds of the way down the English text. See if you can follow along with me, Mr. Dzakula. He says: "Regardless of the fact that practically in the territory of all Serbian Krajinas, we basically reached together with the Yugoslav national army the Territorial Defence and the Serbian volunteers' detachments, the borders of those territories where the Serbian people -- where the Serbian people present an ethnic majority ..." And he says on to say: " ... we have a large and complex task ..." Now, my first question is whether this is consistent with your own knowledge of the composition of the Serb forces that were present in Croatia and the Krajinas during this period, Yugoslav national army, Territorial Defence, and Serbian volunteers.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, they acted together in the area, and they were keeping a certain area under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, then on page 22 for you, Mr. Dzakula, page 16 of the English. Again, this is Mr. Kostic speaking. This is toward the top of the English. Kostic says: "... if Slobodan Milosevic had not gone to The Hague, he probably would have been here today, because it was our intention to ask him to join -- to come and join in our efforts." Mr. Dzakula, the question here is if you could just in a few sentences describe what was the role of Serbia and President Milosevic in respect of these discussions and the consideration of the Vance Plan. What role did Yugoslavia play?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, I think the role of Yugoslavia and primarily Slobodan Milosevic was crucial for the adoption of the Vance Plan, because the leaders of Eastern Slavonia and SAO Krajina were initially opposed to any adoption of the Vance Plan. Therefore, they exerted themselves as much as they could in the Presidency of Yugoslavia and other republics to convince the leaderships that the Vance Plan was the best and, at the moment, the only solution. They explained that at length. Very long meetings were held. And they did that with the aim to convince the political police and military leaders of the SAO Krajina and Eastern Slavonia that the Vance Plan was the only possible option and that it should be adopted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about that more. The next part I'd like to take you to is paragraph -- excuse me, page 37 for you. I think it's toward the bottom, Mr. Dzakula. Twenty-seven and 28 of the English. And on this page, we see that Goran Hadzic starts speaking.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And here he makes reference to some contacts he'd had with a man named Henry Wynaendts in The Hague and in Paris, and he's talking about what Wynaendts had said. My question was whether you were aware that during these months, the late months of 1991, Mr. Hadzic was involved in negotiations and talks with people like Mr. Wynaendts who were members of the international community?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this, because the media reported about it in detail so that the people would be informed about what was being prepared and negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge and what you observed, was Mr. Hadzic's participation in international negotiations something that Mr. Milosevic and the Serbian leadership supported and approved?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. They supported the talks and the negotiations which Mr. Goran Hadzic had with international representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving down a couple of short paragraphs, Mr. Hadzic states: "I would agree with the statement that Yugoslavia should be preserved by means of sending the army back to the Republic of Croatia, even in the bigger extent than before." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Does this relate to the conversation that you'd had or reflect the conversation you'd had with Mr. Hadzic earlier in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. It corresponds with the positions he expressed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then in the next paragraph, he says: "We are being given promises for something that already is the case in our territories with the exception of a small part of Western Slavonia - the ZNG is not present in the Krajinas." Now, my first question is he -- you've described the situation in Western Slavonia at the end of 1991 and how it -- tell us again how it differed from the situation on the ground in the other two SAOs, Krajina, and SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: By contrast with the SAO Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and the other Krajina, which were militarily under the control of the JNA and the Territorial Defence, the whole areas which were envisaged, and as for Western Slavonia, it was perhaps only one-third of the territory of the declared SAO Western Slavonia was under the control of the Territorial Defence and the Yugoslav People's Army, which means that more than two-thirds of the territory was under the control of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just quickly, there's a reference, I think, we haven't dealt with yet. He refers to the ZNG, the ZNG. What is that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The National Guard Corps was actually the corps of the future Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the ZNG at the time was the Croatian National Guard.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, Mr. Hadzic says that in his region they'd placed the TO within the structure of the armed forces and he could not allow the discussion on a subject treating equally the JNA and Ustasha units, the ZNG. And he makes a reference to -- he says: "It is stated here that the JNA and the ZNG are being disarmed." Do you know what was Mr. Hadzic's position on disarmament under the Vance Plan, at least at the time of this discussion in early December 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Initially in the first talks about the Vance Plan, Goran Hadzic was not in favour of the disarmament on part of the JNA or for the adoption of the Vance Plan as it had been envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if you can now go to page 112, Mr. Dzakula. Page 83 of the English. Mr. Dzakula, here -- we see here that you make a statement. That's what I'd like to draw your attention to. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You say here that -- you refer to your brothers from Krajina who liberate their own territories and strongly maintain them within the borders lines. What was your -- why were you making these statements about the situation in Western Slavonia? What's the point you're trying to make here?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to point out to the problems about the Vance Plan which did not cover the areas which I mention here as the ones where the UN should be deployed on the one hand. On the other, I wanted to try to and explain to them that the peace process should be used for the return of refugees to the entire area where war had been waged and that for that we needed tolerance, and we also needed the acceptance of the entire Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of this meeting, were you satisfied with the military situation on the ground, the status quo, on this day, the 9th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: No, I was not satisfied at all, because the military solution, in my view, was no solution at all. It was unnecessary. But once we had it, I was dissatisfied because many areas remained unprotected, and there were no UN representatives there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, was your view shared by Mr. Hadzic for the SBWS; and also, what was the view of the SAO Krajina people here, Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: They showed a form of egotism. They were satisfied because the area where they lived was resolved very well. But that did not resolve satisfactorily the entire Serbian question within the Republic of Croatia, including Western Slavonia. Let me repeat: The Vance Plan offered wider possibilities than what they wanted to achieve by their military plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution offers 65 ter 770, the transcript of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit Number P28. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have the usher's assistance to remove that one and -- but we're going to move to another transcript of another meeting. This is 65 ter 791. Tab -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Twenty-one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Twenty-one. Thank you. I'm not good with numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I believe you've also had an opportunity to review this document in advance; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is this the Presidency meeting minutes from the 12th of December now, three days later, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as indicated here, was -- do you recall was President Slobodan Milosevic present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were present?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I was present too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall if Mr. Hadzic was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I think that he did not attend that meeting, either he or Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And on that point, Mr. Dzakula, if you could go to the page that in your version is marked with page 168 at the top. Page 24 of the English. I believe there that, in fact, President Milosevic notes that neither Mr. Hadzic and Babic are present. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, where he notes that and wonders where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what was the purpose of this meeting, or what were the main -- what was the main topic of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Once again, the topic was the Vance Plan and how to convince the leaders of these areas, that is to say the SAO Krajinas, to accept it as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you'll go to page 179. Page 32 of the English. You'll see that President Milosevic makes some statements about the Vance Plan. If you could just tell us, Mr. Dzakula, what was President Milosevic's position on the Vance Plan at this time, 12th of December?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: At the time, Slobodan Milosevic advocated that there was no alternative for the Vance Plan and that, at the moment, it was the best possible solution, that it should be accepted in the interests of the Serbs in the Krajinas or the SAO areas so that they could live on peacefully rather than continuing with armed conflict and war, because there was no strength for that anymore, either in the army or among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now -- excuse me. If you'll move ahead to page 194 of yours. Page 43 of the English. Now, you've indicated Mr. -- it's been noted that Mr. Babic is not present. Here Milan Martic speaks, and based on this text, could you, in your own recollection, could you tell the Chamber what was the position of Mr. Martic and the SAO Krajina in respect of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: At this meeting, Mr. Milan Martic presented the positions of the Assembly and government of the then-SAO Krajina, which were not willing to accept the Vance Plan. They did not want to change the decision because they were not willing to make any changes. They were afraid of the responsibility that they would have to accept, and they insisted on the position that they couldn't do anything or change their position to the Vance Plan without appropriate decisions, and that was why Milan Babic did not come to attend the meeting. They were afraid to make any concessions at this meeting without his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now if you'll move on to page 212, 212 of yours, page 56 of the English, where we see remarks made by you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: One hundred and twelve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Two hundred and twelve.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Two hundred and twelve. Yes, I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on page 57 of the English, it's about the fourth paragraph of your comments, Mr. Dzakula. You say that: "I do not wish to influence you, but if there is a problem in Western Slavonia, why does it have to be the case with other territories as well? You probably cannot understand and realise it yet, because you have not been in such a situation." Again, you're talking about the situation in Western Slavonia. What was your position on whether the Vance Plan should be accepted for Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: We in the Western Slavonia accepted the Vance Plan. It was perhaps easier for us because our military representatives did not put up any resistance because they had lost territories in the field, in the military sense of the word. And we realised that even though not the entire area was covered by the Vance Plan, I mean Orahovica, Slatina, and Pozega as I said earlier, we did realise that the Vance Plan did not have any alternative, that it should be accepted, and that only with it we could have permanent peace and return refugees to the area. We wanted to help them to realise that the fact that they at the moment had a specific area under their control was not permanent, that they should accept the Vance Plan in order to stop any further conflict, and it was possible to implement the peace plan and return refugees to the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And finally at the very end of the meeting, page 96 of the English, page 268 of the original text, Mr. Kostic here --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: What was the page? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Two sixty-eight. It's the very end. It's the very last page.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Here Mr. Kostic notes again that Babic and Hadzic were not present. Do you know whether Hadzic and Babic then appeared and participated in any subsequent meetings at the Presidency about the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. There were other meetings, and there was a big one that lasted for 52 hours which was attended by both Goran Hadzic and Milan Babic, as well as many others, where the acceptance of the Vance Plan was discussed, and also its pros and cons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this meeting occurred, the 52-hour meeting that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: It was held at some point in mid-January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P29. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 65 ter 3467, and this is a short document that we can work with on the screen, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question here, Mr. Dzakula, is if you recall, then, whether disagreement between Mr. Babic and Mr. Milosevic with regard to the Vance Plan spilled out into the public and the result of this on Mr. Milosevic's relationship with Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, it's clear that through the media Milosevic settled his accounts publicly with Milan Babic, and the message was that he could not keep the Serbs from Krajina as hostages of his policy. And the message in the media was also a message to those were like-minded and everybody who supported him. The consequence of all this was that Mr. Milan Babic was politically removed and could no longer play the leading role in the area of the SAO Krajina or in the main activities in the following period. He was rejected both by the Assembly and the people in the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just for the record, the document we're looking at here, 3467, these are two letters, one published by Babic, and then a response published by President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. Correspondence between Milan Babic and Slobodan Milosevic began at this point. And Milan Babic turned out to be a weak opponent; whereas, Slobodan Milosevic won a political victory and eliminated Milan Babic from the political activities in the Krajina area for the next several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders 3467.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think I misspoke. The original -- the first letter was Mr. President Milosevic and then the response came from Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, may I ask one clarification from the witness. Mr. Witness. Mr. Dzakula, you said that Mr. Babic was removed. And my question is replaced by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He used to be the president of the SAO Krajina, which ceased to exist several days after that, because on the 26th of February, Goran Hadzic became the president of the republic, and the Assembly, which had a session about the acceptance of Vance Plan, was chaired by Milan Paspalj without the presence of Milan Babic. So he wasn't present, nor did he have an opportunity to say anything. This is why I think that he was politically marginalised at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we are going to go into that in more detail in the next few exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, if we could now put up 65 ter 910, please. And this -- we can see if it will work on the screen. Maybe it is faster. Mr. Dzakula, do you see this document? Can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. This is from the meeting of the Presidency. These are the stenographic notes of the meeting held on the 29th of January, 1992, commencing at 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher's assistance. It might actually be faster to work with the paper version because we are going to be moving around this document. It's tab number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, we don't see your name in the first part of this document. Do you know or do you recall whether, in fact, you were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I really cannot recall at this moment about this 29th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple questions about it anyway. And as we see on the bottom, toward the bottom of the first page, item number 1 on the agenda is a report by Mr. Jovic on his visit to the United Nations in the US. Now, if you could go to page 11, Mr. Dzakula, and the rest of us to page 6.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic is speaking, and he's referring to discussions with Cyrus Vance. Do you know who Cyrus Vance was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. He's the one who conceived the peace plan for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then there's a reference also to a Goulding, and I think you mentioned him already.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I did, yes. He was the UN under-secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And here in this section there's discussion about what laws will apply inside of what would be these UN-protected territories. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then on paragraph 7 of the English, and for you, Mr. Dzakula, the bottom of page 12, they're suggesting that Goulding should talk to Babic and Hadzic, and now he's going to talk to Dzakula too.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Babic. Babic. I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether discussions took place between Mr. Goulding, and Messrs. Babic and Hadzic about the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I think that it was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And did you have any discussions yourself with Mr. Goulding?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In April 1992, later, I had talks with Mr. Goulding regards the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Dzakula, if you'd go to page 22. It's page 12 of the English. And now for -- in the English version, it's the bottom half of page 12. And here Mr. Jovic is saying that he'd been informed about his talks with Hadzic, Babic, and Tudjman, and he indicates that Goran Hadzic had accepted the plan but requested clarification.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then he goes on to describe the talks between Goulding and Babic, indicating that Babic --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I see that as well. I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then continuing on to the next page in English, the end of the paragraph where he says that Babic rejected the plan. So the question here, Mr. Dzakula, is: Again, based on your own involvement, I know you weren't present at this meeting but you were involved in these discussions generally, does this accurately set out the positions of Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Babic in respect of the peace plan now at this time, which is 29th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it does refer to the positions, because Mr. Hadzic accepted the Vance Plan, but Mr. Babic never did. He was always against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then moving on to page 14 of the English, and, Mr. Dzakula, I think for you this is page 23. The paragraph that begins with "As for Babic, we will assume a political obligation ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: No, I still don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read the sentence, and perhaps you'll be able to find it. "As for Babic, we will assume a political obligation to continue to talk and create a political climate to overcome this issue ... as it has been done in Eastern and Western Slavonia."

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This is on page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I found it, yes. I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This reference to creating a political climate to overcome the issue, what's that a reference to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, this is in reference to the political elimination of Milan Babic, because he was very firm in his rejection of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And now, Mr. Dzakula, if you will move down about seven paragraphs, you'll see that one of the participants here, Petar Gracanin, speaks.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And he makes a reference to you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, he does mention me in a very short sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've told us what your position was, and then Borislav Jovic says: "We will talk with Dzakula, so we will have two for and one against. Now, they will accept Dzakula so that we can have this politically for the public, that there are two Krajinas and that for the time being one remains." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So does that accurately reflect the way that ultimately the issue of -- the position on the Vance Plan was resolved among the Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it does reflect the way we accepted this immediately without any immediate to convince us so that there was no need for this conversation that is mentioned here, because they knew our position. We were in favour of that, whereas Milan Babic from the SAO Krajina was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution tenders 65 ter 910.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P31. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 65 ter 5139.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you would not have seen this at the time, but have you seen that document in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is a cable to the UN Secretary-General from Mr. Goulding, and he's a sending a copy to Cyrus Vance, and it's dated 28 January 1992. So just the day before the transcript that we just discussed. Now, here in paragraph 2, Mr. Goulding describes the results or the outcome of his discussions with Mr. Hadzic and Babic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is where he sets out the position on the Vance Plan as he understood it to be from them, that is reflecting the position of Hadzic and Babic here in items (a) through (e).

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I see that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then just moving ahead to the next page. In paragraph 3, then Mr. Goulding sets out his response to the various objections that had been raised by Hadzic and Babic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 4 he says that: "On the basis of these clarifications and especially (a) above, Hadzic said that he accepted the plan and would co-operate with the UN force. However, Babic and his team would not be moved."

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So based on what you knew and your involvement in the various discussions on the Vance Plan, Mr. Dzakula, is the information set out in this document an accurate reflection of the various positions, clarifications among the parties during this time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. This document accurately reflects the state of affairs and how things were happening at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution moves into evidence 5139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be assigned Exhibit Number P32. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 3459.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzakula, the English in this exhibit is the original language version of the document, but it appears to have been written by Mr. Babic. It's dated February 9th of 1992. Do you know about this document? Do you know what this is -- were you aware of -- of what's described in this letter?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. I know what was happening. These were last attempts by Mr. Babic to convince the international community that the Assemblies that were going to be held adopting the Vance Plan were illegal, because he wanted his positions to be respected. He could not stop the inevitable process from happening and the will of the Krajina people to accept the Vance Plan, but he wanted to represent this as illegal and illegitimate, which was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this letter, Mr. Babic makes reference to an Assembly in a place called Glina. If you know, what happened in Glina at this Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The SAO Krajina Assembly was held in Glina which accepted unanimously the Vance Plan as a solution for the area of the former Yugoslavia, and so the SAO Krajina accepted the Vance Plan so none of the representatives who were there would, in future, oppose the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And there's a reference in the second paragraph to General Adzic and Branko Kostic from Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav Presidency, having come to Glina. Do you know if that took place?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. They came to explain to the people, to convince them of the -- their safety, that Yugoslavia would give them their support. When the people representing Yugoslavia came to them to Glina, it was a message that they would not be left alone, that they were going to help. And it was a message to the leadership that was going to accept the Vance Plan that they were not alone in doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution moves 3459 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P33. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, the next exhibit I want to know you is actually a short video-clip that is 65 ter 4809. It's now been given the number 4809.2 to distinguish it from a different clip that the Chamber saw yesterday from the same video, and so we can just take a moment to get ourselves into Sanction. Okay. Let's -- if we can now run this clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] All that has been happening, as you said, the last few days is very sad, but unfortunately anticipated. I have been expecting it since I have some bad experiences with the work of the party whose Main Board member I was and with the events that occurred in Knin two years ago, similar to those here and now. Our stand, our government's stand, is that the unity of the Serb people --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. We cut off the very first part of it. I think the audio wasn't quite up. And if we -- if we may, I'd like to start it again from the beginning so that we can take the reporter's question, the question that Mr. Hadzic is responding to here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] "Journalist: Mr. Prime Minister, the attitude of the government of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem on past events, the Glina Assembly, the Knin Assembly, the letter of Dr. Milan Babic to Boutros-Ghali, its dismissal and everything that was happening during the last few days. "All that has been happening, as you said, the last few days is very sad, but unfortunately it's anticipated. I was expecting it since I have had some bad experiences with the work of a party whose Main Board I was and with events that occurred in Knin two years ago, and similar to those here and now. Our stand, our government's stand, is that the unity of the Serb people must not be questioned in any case. We are respecting the majority will of the Assembly representatives, that is the Serb Assembly in Glina, and we shall adhere to that will, whatever they decided is what we shall be devoted to. "When you mentioned the Assembly, there is the Assembly of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem in Bela Crkva, there is the Assembly in Knin, actually in Glina, which is having sessions the last couple of days. There are differences in the constitution of either Assembly on the level of the Serb Republic of Krajina. What is all this about? "Goran Hadzic: Our government is currently preparing for the arrival of the Blue Helmets, it is clear that there can be no peace in these areas unless the Blue Helmets arrive, or if total war should continue until the Ustasha's army is utterly defeated, only then there could be peace. Otherwise, in this case, there can be no peace whatsoever. Our opinion is well known, the Blue Helmets should arrive the conditions established for the people to declare its will in a democratic way. The current situation on the frontiers is very complicated, the Ustashas regularly violate the cease-fire, which will continue unless the Blue Helmets arrive shortly. I'm afraid that the Ustashas will completely breach the truce and that the war will continue, with incomprehensible consequences for this part of Europe, maybe even for the whole of Europe. Thus I hope that Boutros-Ghali will today propose that the United Nations come to our area. I have just returned from the Vukovar Hospital, where I visited the wounded who were injured in the meantime, during this violation of the cease-fire. My village was attacked as well, the village I was born in, with artillery fire, and in accordance with the standing orders we did not respond to the firing, since we do not want to be accused. The representatives of the European Community were there, I do not know about the United Nations ones, and they saw that the attack was committed, I do not know if they will judge objectively and say who is to blame. We have not responded to the attack, but I fear that we will have to react in the next case of the violation of the cease-fire, since they were using 155 and 205-millimetre Howitzers, causing horrible destruction. Moreover, I do not know how are we to keep our soldiers from fighting back, since we are being shot at non-stop. "Journalist: This is what they want, to provoke a reaction. "Goran Hadzic: It is clear that they want that, as the arrival of the Blue Helmets, the way it was planned, does not suit them, since the Blue Helmets will pressure them to recognise the system which is constitutionally legal, that is our system, so they do not want to have them. However, we have to be smart enough and have enough patience to maintain the truce, but I say that I fear if the arrival of the Blue Helmets will be postponed, that the cease-fire will not hold. They're now clearing the mines around our territory and will probably attempt a frontal assault with the tanks they unfortunately captured or actually received from some JNA officers and which they are receiving non-stop even from Switzerland and Germany. They are preparing for a war and will probably attempt an assault, but I'm an optimist and believe that should the Blue Helmets arrive in seven to ten days, at least their advance contingent, shall be prevented. Should they not arrive by end of the month, there will be a total war, a war to annihilation, which means that we will probably have to penetrate deeper into the territory now controlled by Croats and then sit around the table to talk. However, I propose that we do so before the clash and that we agree, before the fight begins, on possibly the same issues as we will anyway have to, but after the large losses. There are huge losses that should have been avoided, had this been respected ... our proposals and our will, the things we propose before the war, namely that the Serb people in Croatia have -- were not supposed to be an ethnic minority and did not want to live, these Serbs in their ethnic regions did not want to live in Croatia but in Yugoslavia instead, as they had already declared twice, that is either in Serbia or in Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, just a couple of questions about this and then we can finish for the day. First of all, the footage here, do you recognise this television footage? Does it appear to be from the region?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I do recognise this speech by Mr. Hadzic. This was somewhere in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, earlier we looked at the letter that Mr. Babic wrote to Boutros-Ghali on the 9th of February, 1992, and the whole incident of Mr. Babic being moved out of the way, if I can put it like that. Does it appear that that's what Mr. Hadzic is talking about in this video when he's asked questions?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the clip, he was talking about the event in Glina, an unfortunate incident as far as he was concerned, and that unity was necessary, and he said that there were always problems when he went to Knin, that that reminded him of events from before. So this is a discussion about this process of the political elimination of Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you were president of the SAO Western Slavonia at the time. During these days, 1991, early 1992, did you wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: No, I never wore a uniform or had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as the president of the government of the one of the SAOs, did you consider public statements about a war to the annihilation or making a deeper penetration into the territory controlled by Croats, statements like that would promote the Vance Plan, the peace process that was being discussed at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, I did not tend to give such statements. It never occurred to me to do that. Had I ever given a statement of that kind, that would have been played on Croatian television every day in a desire to present me as an extremist. I knew that nothing would come out of making extremist statements and that tolerant dialogue was required in order to reach some sort of understanding and solution between Serbs and Croats. Extremist statements only encouraged hostilities, such as that event and other events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can -- this is actually a very good time for us to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this -- have you finished with this video footage, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have, and we tender it. My apologies. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P34. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dzakula, this is the end of your testimony for today, but only for today. You will come back tomorrow at 9.00 in this same courtroom, and you are still under oath. That means that you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody, and you're not allowed to talk to any of the parties until the end of your testimony. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The court usher will now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- escort you out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of October, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.03 p.m.,
